name: Display rings turning both ways
returns: a new grid, as a list of lists
brief:
A departures board is a grid of tiles, `grid[i][j]`, split into rings from the outside in: ring 0 is the border, ring 1 the border of what is left, and so on. Each ring turns `k` steps. Ring 0 turns clockwise, ring 1 anticlockwise, and the directions keep alternating. One step moves every tile of a ring to the next cell along that ring.

When what is left in the middle is a single row, a single column or a single tile, it is not a ring and stays where it is.

Write `turn_rings(grid, k)`, which returns the new grid and leaves `grid` unchanged.

Example. For `grid = [[4, 7, 1], [9, 5, 2], [8, 3, 6]]` and `k = 1`, the border turns one step clockwise and the centre tile stays. The answer is `[[9, 4, 7], [8, 5, 1], [3, 6, 2]]`.
constraints: At most $100$ rows and $100$ columns, every row the same length, and $0 \le k \le 10^9$.
$O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$ time is the target, whatever `k`. Turning one step at a time is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: List the cells of each ring in clockwise order. A ring of `n` cells is back where it started after `n` steps, so only `k % n` steps matter, and an anticlockwise turn of `k` is a clockwise turn of `-k % n`.

examples.note: The eight border tiles move one place clockwise; the centre is a single tile and stays.
The border turns clockwise and the inner 2 by 2 ring anticlockwise.

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The change from turning every ring one way is the alternating direction and the rule that a leftover row or column stays put. So each ring needs its own sign, and the loop stops before a ring of one line.
solution:
def turn_rings(grid, k):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    out = [row[:] for row in grid]
    t = 0
    while rows - 2 * t >= 2 and cols - 2 * t >= 2:
        top, left, bottom, right = t, t, rows - 1 - t, cols - 1 - t
        cells = [(top, j) for j in range(left, right)]
        cells += [(i, right) for i in range(top, bottom)]
        cells += [(bottom, j) for j in range(right, left, -1)]
        cells += [(i, left) for i in range(bottom, top, -1)]
        n = len(cells)
        shift = k % n if t % 2 == 0 else -k % n
        for idx, (i, j) in enumerate(cells):
            a, b = cells[(idx + shift) % n]
            out[a][b] = grid[i][j]
        t += 1
    return out
notes: A ring of `n` cells repeats every `n` steps, so turning it `k` steps is the same as turning it `k % n` steps.
The rings stop when the middle is one row, one column or one tile; reading that as a ring would visit its cells twice.
Each cell is read and written once, so the work is $O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$, whatever `k`.
